casuallab.title: Who should get the offer?
casuallab.why: A discount can increase activity. The harder question is whether a model can identify who will respond—and spend the same budget better.
casuallab.finding: The complex targeting model has not earned its advantage.
casuallab.method: I test effect estimates against known answers, then compare spending rules at the same budget in simulated markets held out from training.
casuallab.takeaway: The learner misses the recovery benchmark. In the budget experiment, a uniform allocation also produces more incremental trips than the model-based rule.
casuallab.boundary: Semi-synthetic validation, not a measured effect of a real NYC promotion. The oracle knows the true average effect; it is a test benchmark, not a deployable policy.

charts.title: The model misses the simple benchmark
charts.subtitle: Effect-estimation error · lower is better
charts.caption: The targeting model has more error than a constant benchmark that knows the true average effect. This test does not support a claim that the model reliably identifies who benefits more.

charts.title: Equal budgets, no targeting advantage
charts.subtitle: Incremental trips · eight held-out simulated markets
charts.caption: With a budget of 1,000 in each market, the model-based policy averages 64.50 extra trips versus 68.50 for uniform allocation. These are simulated policy outcomes, not field-experiment estimates.

macroeconomics.title: Would the forecast work in real time?
macroeconomics.why: Economic statistics are revised after publication. A model can look better in hindsight if its backtest uses numbers no one knew at the time.
macroeconomics.finding: Changing the data vintage changes which models look best.
macroeconomics.method: I reconstruct official release histories and rerun forecasts with three information rules: data known then, revised values with the same availability, and unrestricted latest values.
macroeconomics.takeaway: Only the strict as-of rule avoids both future releases and future revisions. Even holding availability fixed, revised values change the GDP ranking of all six models.
macroeconomics.boundary: The fixed-mask comparison is a hindsight diagnostic, not a valid real-time forecast. Results describe this pilot and its final holdout; they do not establish a universally best model.

charts.title: Hindsight enters through two doors
charts.subtitle: 7,985 feature cells audited under each rule
charts.caption: Strict as-of uses only information known at the time. Fixed mask keeps the original release availability but imports 5,464 later revisions. Unrestricted latest values also introduce 863 future releases. The two counts can overlap; do not add them.

charts.title: All six GDP models change rank
charts.subtitle: Same availability; different data revisions · 8 final holdout forecasts · horizon 0
charts.caption: In the final GDP holdout, Elastic Net moves from fourth to first when later revisions replace the original values. AR(1) moves from first to second. Both predictor values and scoring targets are revised, while release availability stays fixed. Eight forecasts (July 2024–April 2026) are too few to establish general model superiority.

realestate.title: Does a cheap mortgage keep a loan in place?
realestate.why: When a new mortgage costs more than the one a homeowner already has, giving up the old loan becomes expensive. I study whether those loans are less likely to be paid off.
realestate.finding: Bigger rate gaps are associated with fewer mortgage exits.
realestate.method: I compare monthly payoff rates across rate gaps, then estimate a complementary log-log hazard model with observed loan and local-market controls.
realestate.takeaway: The adjusted model reports a hazard ratio of 0.817 for a one-percentage-point larger gap. Unweighted sample shares show the broad ordering, but are not population exit probabilities.
realestate.boundary: An association, not a causal estimate. Payoff and maturity are pooled; refinancing-related and sale-related payoff cannot be distinguished. Household moves are not observed. This is a selected Freddie Mac sample.

charts.title: The adjusted association remains negative
charts.subtitle: Complementary log-log model · estimation sample, 2021–2023
charts.caption: A one-percentage-point larger rate gap is associated with an 18.3% lower conditional hazard in this model (1 − 0.817). This is a relative association, not an 18.3-point fall in monthly probability. No confidence interval is displayed; this is not a causal estimate.

charts.title: The sample shows the broad rate-gap pattern
charts.subtitle: Unweighted estimation sample · 2021–2023
charts.caption: Each point is a rate-gap group, placed at its mean gap. The sample overrepresents loans that exit; these unweighted shares are not population monthly probabilities. The downward pattern has reversals and differs from the adjusted model above.

tariff-incidence.title: Who absorbed the tariff?
tariff-incidence.why: When the U.S. raises import tariffs, foreign suppliers could cut their prices—or importers could pay more. The distinction determines who bears the initial cost.
tariff-incidence.finding: The evidence points toward higher costs for U.S. importers.
tariff-incidence.method: I compare each wave of tariffed products with never-tariffed products, tracking unit import values before and after the policy and checking three sample windows.
tariff-incidence.takeaway: Duty-exclusive unit values show no clear offsetting decline. Duty-inclusive unit values rise. This pattern supports importer-side incidence within the sample.
tariff-incidence.boundary: Unit values are not individual transaction prices. The duty-inclusive measure includes the tariff by construction; the pre-duty series is essential. Quantity fails its date-placebo check.

charts.title: Duty-inclusive costs rise; pre-duty values barely move
charts.subtitle: Average post-tariff effect across three sample windows
charts.caption: The pre-duty effect stays close to +0.025 log points in all windows, rather than showing a large supplier-side price cut. Duty-inclusive effects stay near +0.15. Unit values are imperfect price proxies.

charts.title: The divergence appears after the tariff
charts.subtitle: Stacked event study · never-treated products as controls
charts.caption: Thin vertical lines show reported 95% intervals. The omitted reference month is −3. Pre-duty values show no sustained offsetting decline; duty-inclusive values rise after treatment. This figure uses the report’s rounded estimates.

microstructure.title: How much short-horizon edge does order flow carry?
microstructure.why: Order-flow imbalance can anticipate small price moves. Measuring that edge properly means replaying it through realistic execution delays and an explicit fee hurdle.
microstructure.finding: Order flow carries a positive gross edge in 110 of 144 execution scenarios.
microstructure.method: I replay one four-hour BTC/ETH order-book capture across two evaluation phases, four horizons, and nine delay combinations, with a fixed 4 bp fee.
microstructure.takeaway: The best gross edge reaches 2.39 bp, measured against a fixed 4 bp taker fee; lower-cost execution is the next test.
microstructure.boundary: Exploratory simulation · research reference only · not live trading. The 144 scenarios overlap and are not independent experiments or a portfolio to add together.

charts.title: Gross edge across 144 scenarios
charts.subtitle: Each dot is one fee-and-latency scenario · dashed line marks the fixed 4 bp fee
charts.caption: Each dot is one scenario’s gross edge per unit of turnover, sorted from lowest to highest; 110 of 144 are above zero and the best reaches 2.39 bp. The dashed line marks the fixed 4 bp taker fee. Overlapping scenarios must not be summed.

charts.title: Gross edge is positive at every horizon
charts.subtitle: Gross-positive scenarios out of 36 per horizon
charts.caption: At least 22 of 36 scenarios are gross-positive at each horizon, and 35 of 36 at the 100-event horizon. This is one four-hour exploratory capture, not a test of live profitability or cross-day reliability.

em-factor-timing.title: Can machine learning time equity factors?
em-factor-timing.why: Factor returns vary over time. I test whether learned forecasts add value beyond a pooled, shrinkage-mean benchmark in emerging markets.
em-factor-timing.finding: Pooling explains much of the apparent predictability.
em-factor-timing.method: I compare out-of-sample linear, tree, and neural-network forecasts on JKP global factors, test developed-to-emerging-market transfer, and evaluate timing after turnover costs.
em-factor-timing.takeaway: On capped value-weighted factors, all learned forecasts lose to the shrinkage mean on out-of-sample R². At the baseline trading cost, the shrinkage-mean tilt also beats learned timing portfolios.
em-factor-timing.boundary: Out-of-sample predictive association. Results depend on factor weighting and trading costs; equal-weighted factors differ. Factor returns exclude their own rebalancing costs.

charts.title: Shrinkage mean beats every learned timing model on OOS R²
charts.subtitle: Out-of-sample R² vs unpooled own mean (%) · 801,536 country-factor-months
charts.caption: Against the unpooled own mean, every model achieves positive OOS R² (+0.83% to +1.16%), but the non-timing regional shrinkage mean alone reaches +1.20% (t = 9.05). Measured against the shrinkage mean, all learned models have negative OOS R².

charts.title: Shrinkage-mean tilt leads net Sharpe after turnover costs
charts.subtitle: Annualized Sharpe ratio net of 20 bp turnover cost · 2000–2025 OOS
charts.caption: Because learned timing rules turn over 41%–61% per month versus 6.1% for the shrinkage-mean tilt, the shrinkage-mean portfolio achieves the highest net Sharpe (1.91) ahead of static equal weight (1.48) and GBRT (1.26).

polymarket-factors.title: Which prediction-market signals survive a realistic backtest?
polymarket-factors.why: Bounded prices, early settlement, and stale quotes can create apparent predictability. I study which cross-sectional signals remain after correcting those artifacts.
polymarket-factors.finding: Reversal, volatility, and illiquidity survive the corrections.
polymarket-factors.method: I study 4,000 Polymarket markets, remove five backtest artifacts, control for price levels, and evaluate factor signs on a held-out half of the panel.
polymarket-factors.takeaway: Five backtest artifacts inflate 30-day momentum IC eightfold (−0.440 to −0.054); price-neutral OOS ICs remain significant for illiquidity (−0.072), volatility (−0.069), and reversal (−0.032).
polymarket-factors.boundary: Backtest association, not live execution. Capacity is roughly $100–200 per position. The combined strategy weight was chosen in sample, and daily-close fills omit intraday slippage.

charts.title: Illiquidity, volatility, and reversal survive price-level controls
charts.subtitle: Out-of-sample price-neutral rank IC · 54 five-day periods across 4,000 markets
charts.caption: After residualizing on [1, p, p²], illiquidity (PM-LIQ, IC = −0.072), low volatility (PM-VOL, −0.069), 30-day reversal (PM-MOM, −0.032), and time-to-resolution (PM-TTR, −0.028) remain statistically significant out of sample.

charts.title: Five backtest artifacts inflate naive momentum IC eightfold
charts.subtitle: 30-day momentum raw IC across progressive artifact-removal stages
charts.caption: Percentage returns near zero, extreme price bounds, same-bar bounce, pre-settlement drift, and stale non-executable quotes inflate the apparent 30-day reversal IC from −0.440 to −0.054 raw (−0.032 price-neutral).

crypto-factors.title: Do equity microstructure factors travel to crypto?
crypto-factors.why: Crypto offers open minute-bar and perpetual-futures data. I test whether ideas from an A-share microstructure research series carry over to this different market.
crypto-factors.finding: Most factors do not travel; funding and positioning hold up better.
crypto-factors.method: I test cross-sectional factors on 105 coins, check split samples and parameters, compare funding on OKX, and track the composite after publication.
crypto-factors.takeaway: Funding (+1.42 Sharpe), retail positioning (+1.39), and a low-price range factor (+1.63) support a market-neutral composite in the 730-day panel. Post-publication windows include both gains and losses.
crypto-factors.boundary: Backtest and out-of-sample backtest association, not live trading. Next-close fills omit market impact; the sample is an altcoin bear market and the OKX check is short.

charts.title: Funding, retail positioning, and low-price range transfer to crypto
charts.subtitle: 730-day daily quintile long–short Sharpe (net of 5 bp/side) · 105 coins
charts.caption: Low-price range (+1.63), funding-rate contrarian carry (+1.42), and retail long/short positioning (+1.39) hold up across the 730-day Binance panel and OKX cross-validation, while cross-sectional momentum (−0.38) fails to transfer.

charts.title: Post-publication out-of-sample windows include both gains and drawdowns
charts.subtitle: Frozen 3-factor composite return (%) across 92 post-publication days (Jun–Aug 2026)
charts.caption: Tracked out of sample without re-fitting after the May 2026 cutoff, the equal-weight composite gained +4.57% in June 2026 before losing −6.93% in July and −3.97% in August (−6.55% cumulative), underscoring regime sensitivity.
